Data Resource Profile: A Florida-scale simulated dataset for developing and benchmarking record-linkage software for cancer data systems

Authors
Affiliations

Abraham D. Flaxman

University of Washington

Anders Alexandersson

University of Miami Miller School of Medicine

Abstract

Introduction … Methods … Results … Conclusion …

Keywords

record linkage, entity resolution, simulated data, cancer registry, benchmark dataset, reproducibility, pseudopeople

Key Features

  • What is unique: a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a simulant_id, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly rather than estimated), designed to capture the record matching challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system.

  • Why created: linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing.

  • Details: a simulated Florida drawn from the 50,518,675 simulated people recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 censuses, including a simulated registry of 5,000,000 records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher finder files of 500,000 and 100,000 records drawn from residents in 2040.

  • Data linkage: the larger finder file includes 100,000 people who are also in the registry and the smaller finder file includes 20,000. There is no overlap between the finder files.

  • Main categories of data: simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications).

  • Access: direct download under a permissive licence with a DOI.

2 Methods

This section describes the simulated population and the Florida extract we cut from it (Section 2.1), how the three files were drawn from that extract (Section 2.2), the noise they carry and the form they are released in (Section 2.3), the checks the build makes on itself (Section 2.4), and the measures that Section 3 reports (Section 2.5). The mechanics that matter only to someone rebuilding the files, hash expressions, trimming rules, file formats, are collected in Section 7.

2.1 Source population and the Florida extract

The records come from pseudopeople, a Python package for generating simulated versions of the data sets that record linkage runs on [1,2]. Behind it is a microsimulation of the United States, initialised to the size and demographics of the country in 2020 and run forward through 2040 with births, deaths and moves, in which each simulated person, a “simulant” in pseudopeople’s vocabulary, carries a simulant_id and is observed by simulated data-collecting systems: a decennial census in 2020, 2030 and 2040, the Social Security Administration, tax filings and others [2]. The package ships with a small sample population, which is all this document executes (the listing below shows the interface); the full population is available on request [3].

Code 
import pseudopeople as psp
census = psp.generate_decennial_census()   # the bundled sample population, 2020 census
census.head()
simulant_id household_id first_name middle_initial last_name age date_of_birth street_number street_name unit_number city state zipcode housing_type relationship_to_reference_person sex race_ethnicity year
0 0_2 0_7 Diana P Kofron 25 05/06/1994 5112 145th st NaN Anytown WA 00000 Household Reference person Female White 2020
1 0_3 0_7 Anna A Kofron 25 09/29/1994 5112 145th st NaN Anytown WA 00000 Household Other relative Female White 2020
2 0_923 0_8033 Gerald R Butler 76 11/03/1943 1130 mallory ln NaN Anytown WA 00000 Household Reference person Male Black 2020
3 0_2641 0_1066 Loretta T Carley 61 07/71/1958 NaN delacorte dr NaN Anytown WA 00000 Household Reference person Female White 2020
4 0_2801 0_1138 Richard R Jones 73 03/03/1947 950 caribou lane NaN Anytown WA 00000 Household Reference person Male White 2020

pseudopeople can generate one state and year of the census directly, but it has no interface for the sampling design we needed, quotas by age and sex and controlled overlaps between files, and its Social Security observer has no state filter, so we did the selection ourselves. With DuckDB 1.5.4 we read the census observer’s Parquet files directly, kept the Florida rows of the three censuses, one per person per census, and built two pools from them. The “last-seen pool” holds every person ever recorded in Florida, taken once at their latest census, and is the frame for the simulated registry; it is more than twice the size of Florida’s population at any one census, because it keeps everyone who died or left the state between censuses, which is what a registry does with the cases it has registered. The residents of 2040 are the frame for the finder files, since a researcher’s cohort is a roster of living people at one time. SSNs are joined from the Social Security observer on the identifier, and pseudopeople is then run only on the rows we selected (Section 7), which is what makes a Florida-scale build a matter of minutes rather than a pass over the national files. Addresses in the source are real Florida city names and ZIP codes with simulated streets, so the released addresses place people in real cities at no real location [2], and the simulation knows nothing about cancer: the registry is a sample of people chosen to have a registry’s age and sex pattern, not a model of disease.

2.2 Cohort design and sampling

The design targets live in one configuration file: a simulated registry of 5,000,000 people with the age and sex distribution of the cases FCDS reported between 1995 and 2023 [4], and finder files of 500,000 and 100,000 people, of whom 100,000 and 20,000 also appear in the registry, with no person in both finder files. The age and sex target is the count column of an FCDS table of reported cases by sex and 18 age groups, taken as shares, and each of the 36 strata contributes an exact quota, filled by a reproducible draw within the stratum (Section 7). We prefer the registry’s own case shares to a general population target because they are the age and sex pattern a linkage against FCDS meets, and matching them is what forces a pool with the dead and departed in it, since a single census has too few older men to supply five million people with that pattern. The cost is that registry records carry the vintage of a person’s last census, realistic for a registry but no longer a snapshot of one year’s residents, and that three censuses span twenty years where FCDS’s caseload spans four decades. The 20% overlap is the second author’s reading of the finder files FCDS receives, which often overlap the registry by about that much or less, and a much smaller overlap would leave too few true pairs to score a method on.

Overlap members are drawn from the registry members whose last census is 2040, so that a person’s registry record and finder record are the same census record, and the rest of each finder file from that year’s residents outside the registry. Because pseudopeople’s row noise removes an unpredictable number of rows, every cohort is drawn oversize, noised, and trimmed back to its exact target by a seeded rule that also keeps the finder files disjoint (Section 7). A registry row and a finder row that carry the same identifier are a “true pair”, the unit every linkage result is scored on, and every other pairing of a registry row with a finder row is a true non-match; people last seen in 2020 or 2030 appear in the registry alone, and are the non-matches a linkage must reject. A true pair is one source record noised twice, under different seeds for the registry (42) and the finder files (1), so its two records differ only by injected noise, with no move, ageing or change of surname between them. This is the simplest choice and the easiest case a linkage can face; it is weighed in Section 4, and the pool keeps every census year, so drawing an overlap member’s registry record from an earlier census is a small change to the overlap draw alone.

2.3 Noise, schema and packaging

The noise is pseudopeople’s default suite, in which each column carries several mechanisms at 1% of cells apiece (a first name can be left blank, replaced by a nickname or a fake name, or altered by a phonetic, optical-character-recognition or typing error; a date of birth can have its month and day swapped, digits miswritten or be copied from a household member; a categorical field can take a wrong category) and rows go missing by non-response at 1.45%, with two additions. We raised the blanking of the six address fields to 5% in the finder files and left it at 1% in the registry, and we handled the SSN ourselves, because pseudopeople does not noise that column in the census: SSNs are blanked to a target share of 20% in the finder files and 5% in the registry, counting the people who never held a number in the simulation before blanking anyone else, and 1% of the finder files’ remaining SSNs have one adjacent pair of digits swapped, a mechanism pseudopeople lacks (Section 7). These rates are the second author’s specification of what a researcher’s finder file looks like against the registry’s consolidated file, which is usually the cleaner of the two [5], and we do not defend them as realistic beyond that. What they leave out is as important as what they include: the SSN carries no wrong digits and no relative’s number, no surname changes, the noise is symmetric between the files and independent across fields where a real cohort has habits of its own, and both files share one format exactly; these are weighed in Section 4. pseudopeople’s row duplication, which gives a child a second row at a guardian’s address, is switched off, so every file has exactly one row per person, and within-file duplicate detection is not something these files exercise.

Every row carries the identifier and the fields linkage relies on: first name, middle initial, last name, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, street number, street name, unit number, city, state, ZIP code and SSN, with race/ethnicity kept because FCDS’s own submission layout carries it [6]. The release covers every field in either of FCDS’s minimum matching sets, but not the layout’s maiden name, alias or birthplace. Registry rows add a diagnosis date, a day drawn uniformly within the year of the record’s census, so that age at diagnosis is within a year of the age the quota was matched on, at the cost that diagnoses heap on three years (Section 4); a finder file is a cohort roster and has no such date. The files are CSV with a header row and blanks as empty fields, a data dictionary travels inside the zip with every field’s format, blank convention and noise mechanisms, the zip is built so that its bytes depend only on its contents, and the deposit adds a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests and the configuration file with every seed and target (Section 7). This profile describes dataset version 0.4, built with pseudopeople 1.2.8.

2.4 Quality assurance

Four checks run with the build or just after it, and their outcomes are reported in Section 3.1 and Section 3.2. Reproducibility: the build is a pure function of the configuration’s seeds, so we built the release twice, on different nodes, and compared the digests of every file. Scale: the 2020 extract is compared with Florida’s official 2020 census count, the one external check available to a simulated population. Composition: the age and sex composition of each file, computed from the source’s true ages rather than the noised dates of birth, is compared with the FCDS shares the registry was drawn to, recording the largest deviation of any stratum, and the finder files’ composition with that of the 2040 Florida pool; agreement with FCDS is a check that the sampler did what it was told, not evidence of fidelity. Face validity: we tabulated the three most common first names in each age and sex group and read a sample of true pairs side by side, which is where the noise mechanisms show themselves one record at a time.

2.5 Characterising the data

Section 3 reports five kinds of measure, all computed on the released files by scripts archived with the pipeline. Error structure: for each field, the share of values blank in each file against the rate set for it and, among true pairs, the share whose two values are present and identical character for character and the share with a blank on either side, together with the count of finder-file SSNs with two adjacent digits swapped, sentinel checks (dates of birth that do not parse as calendar dates, Doe-pattern names, repeated-digit SSNs and SSNs outside the ranges the SSA issues) and SSN blankness by race/ethnicity and by age at diagnosis. Quasi-identifier uniqueness: the share of registry people whose first name, last name and date of birth, last name and date of birth, or ZIP code, date of birth and sex is shared by no one else in the file, and the share who share a full name with someone. A deterministic baseline: 11 exact-agreement rules, each a set of fields, or two sets joined by “or”, on which both records must agree after lower-casing and trimming, scored against the identifier as precision and recall, which we also report as false-match and missed-match rates [7]; we do not rank rules by F1 [8] and omit specificity, which is uninformative when true non-matches grow with the product of the file sizes [9]. The rules include the two field sets FCDS’s Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [10] and the two in its current Data Linkage Record Layout [6], as exact rules and not as FCDS’s own procedure; exact agreement is a floor rather than a straw man, since deterministic algorithms run in production linkages [11,12]. Stratified baselines: three of the rules recomputed within race/ethnicity groups of the finder record; the noise is injected without regard to race, so any differential is inherited from the source population, chiefly through who holds an SSN. Blocking feasibility: the number of candidate pairs and the share of true pairs retained when comparisons are restricted to records that agree on the full date of birth, or on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth, which are the first numbers a probabilistic user needs for planning compute.

3 Results

We describe the released files first (Section 3.1), then the people in them (Section 3.2), the errors in their fields (Section 3.3) and how hard those errors make the files to link with exact rules (Section 3.4).

3.1 Structure, contents, and where the data are held

This data resource is a zip archive containing three comma-separated data files and a data dictionary, to be deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted before publication. The high-level characteristics of the files are described in Table 1: a simulated registry of 5,000,000 people and two finder files of 500,000 and 100,000 people. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 census, a pool of 50,518,675 distinct simulated people. The larger finder file shares 100,000 people with the registry, 20% of its records, and the smaller shares 20,000, the same 20% share; the two finder files share no people with each other, matching the overlap design described above.

The data dictionary inside the archive gives each field’s type, format, blank convention, source and the noise mechanisms that touch it. The deposit also carries a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (Table 1 gives the MD5) and the configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI. A second build from the same configuration and the same source population, which is available on request (Section 5), reproduced all three files byte for byte.

3.2 Population characteristics

The simulated registry closely matches the age and sex distribution of the cases reported to FCDS between 1995 and 2023 [4]. The agreement is within 0.041 percentage points in each of the 36 age and sex strata. 62% of registry records are people aged 65 or older at diagnosis and 4% are under 40; 48% are women. The finder files have the age structure of the simulated population’s Florida residents in 2040 instead: 26% of the larger file are 65 or older, 43% are under 40, and 51% are female.

By race and ethnicity, people in the registry are 64% White, 17% Latino, 12% Black, 5% Asian and 3% other or multiracial (American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial, and unknown), compared with 55%, 21%, 12%, 7% and 4% in the larger finder file. The two finder files differ from each other by at most 0.3 percentage points on every share reported in this section.

The three most common first names in each age group, printed at the ends of the bars in Figure 1, run from Liam, Noah, Oliver among boys under five to James, Robert, John among men of 85 and over, and from Olivia, Charlotte, Emma to Mary, Barbara, Patricia among girls and women.

Figure 2 shows three of the 100,000 people who appear in both the registry and the larger finder file, chosen to show three kinds of error, with every field that differs between their two records marked: a first name recorded as a nickname, with a swapped month and day of birth and errors in three further fields; an address altered in three fields beside a blank SSN; and a swapped month and day of birth beside a swapped pair of SSN digits. The two records of a pair are one census record noised twice, so every difference in the figure is an injected error and not a move or a change of name, a simplification weighed in Section 4.

3.3 Error structure

Table 2 gives the error structure field by field: the share of values that are blank in the registry and in the larger finder file, against the blanking rate set for each, and, among the 100,000 true pairs, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Agreeing exactly means the two values are the same string, character for character. The error structure of the smaller finder file matches that of the larger on every figure in the table to within 0.8 percentage points.

SSNs are blank in 20.0% of finder records, the rate FCDS specified, and in 5.68% of registry records against a specified 5%. The build blanked no registry SSN, so every blank there is a person who never held one in the source population, where coverage varies with age: 3.8% of registry records for people under 40 at diagnosis lack an SSN against 6.4% for people of 40 to 64, and the registry’s ages are the ones with the least coverage, which is why its share sits above both the specification and the whole pool’s 4.18%. Blank SSNs vary by race/ethnicity: in the larger finder file 28.9% of Asian and 23.5% of Latino people’s records have none against 17.8% of White people’s, and in the registry the shares are 21.5%, 15.2% and 1.9%. Of the SSNs present in the larger finder file, 4,001 (1.0%) carry two adjacent digits swapped, and where a true pair has an SSN on both sides the two agree in 99.1% of pairs.

Names and dates of birth disagree more often than SSNs do. Among true pairs with both values present, first names agree in 93.9% of pairs, last names in 96.0% and dates of birth in 93.4%, and each of these fields is blank on one side in about 2.0% of pairs. Taken together, 79.2% of true pairs agree exactly on first name, last name and date of birth, and 77.9% have an SSN on both sides that agrees. Address fields agree in 97.1% of pairs with both present and are blank on one side in 5.9%; the unit number is blank for 94% of registry records, because most addresses have none, and street numbers are blank above their set rates because some source addresses carry none.

Dates of birth are blank in 1.0% of registry records and 1.4% of those present do not parse as a calendar date (such as a month above twelve); 13 registry records carry a Doe-pattern name (John or Jane Doe); no SSN in any file is a single repeated digit; and 52 SSNs in the larger finder file, and none in the registry, fall in ranges the Social Security Administration does not issue.

3.4 Linkage difficulty

Among the 5,000,000 people in the registry, 97.0% have a first name, last name and date of birth that no one else in the file shares, 88.8% have a unique last name and date of birth, and 81.6% a unique ZIP code, date of birth and sex, while 47% share their full name with at least one other person.

Table 3 scores exact-agreement rules on the larger finder file against the key. Agreement on first name, last name and date of birth links 79.2% of true pairs at a precision of 99.81%, and the SSN alone links 77.9% at 99.97%. The two field sets FCDS’s Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [10] behave differently as exact rules: name, SSN and sex makes no false matches and finds 64.7% of true pairs, name with month and year of birth and sex admits 4,421 false matches, 5.5% of the pairs it proposes, and either set finds 81.5%; the two sets of FCDS’s current Data Linkage Record Layout [6], which both require the full date of birth, find 71.7% together with no false matches. Name and date of birth or SSN, the best simple rule, reaches a recall of 95.4% at a precision of 99.82%, and last name with date of birth alone falls to a precision of 71.0%.

Without blocking the two files present 2.5 trillion record pairs. Blocking on the full date of birth leaves 58 million candidate pairs and keeps 91.6% of true pairs, the pairs whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (Table 2); blocking on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth leaves 1.23 billion and keeps 90.7%.

Figure 3 splits three rules by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record. For first name, last name and date of birth the missed-match rate is alike across groups, from 20.1% to 20.9%, and the false-match rate stays below 0.31% in every group. The SSN rule differs by group: it misses 34% of true pairs for Asian people and 29% for Latino people against 19% for White people, and the difference carries into the best simple rule, which misses 7.0% of Asian true pairs against 4.0% of White ones.

The 11 rules run in 3.5 seconds on the 500,000-record file with 8 threads on an eight-core allocation. The 100,000-record file gives the same picture: every rule’s recall is within 0.8 percentage points of the larger file’s.

7 Appendix: technical details of the build

This appendix records the mechanics behind Section 2 for anyone who wants to rebuild the files or a different cut of them; nothing here changes the picture given there. The pipeline is archived with the deposit and every parameter named below lives in its configuration file.

Extraction and staging. DuckDB reads the census observer’s Parquet files directly and keeps the Florida rows of the 2020, 2030 and 2040 censuses, one per person per census. The last-seen pool is each person’s latest of those rows; the finder pool is the rows of 2040. The rows selected for a cohort are written to Parquet ordered by simulant_id before pseudopeople sees them, because pseudopeople walks rows in file order and an unpinned order silently moves the same amount of noise onto different people; the Social Security join is ordered the same way for the same reason. pseudopeople is then run once per file over the staged rows, which is why a Florida-scale build completes in minutes on eight cores.

Reproducible draws. Every sampling decision is a pure function of the record key. A candidate’s rank in a draw is the value of md5_number_lower(simulant_id || ':' || salt || ':' || seed), with the seed 42 and a salt naming the draw, so the registry takes, within each age and sex stratum, the quota members with the smallest hash, and each finder file takes its overlap members from the registry’s 2040 members and its filler from that year’s residents outside the registry by two further salts. We avoided the database’s own random number generator because its results depend on the thread count. Quotas come from the FCDS case shares by largest-remainder rounding, capped at the stratum’s size in the pool.

Oversampling and the stratified trim. pseudopeople’s non-response removes rows, so every cohort is drawn at 1.15 times its target and trimmed after noising with a seeded generator (seed 999) over identifier lists sorted for the same order-dependence reason. The trim takes exactly the target number of overlap members for each finder file, draws filler only from survivors outside the entire overlap pool, and keeps in the registry only the members chosen; an earlier build that trimmed without this stratification kept every surviving overlap candidate and overshot its overlap targets, which is the failure the rule exists to prevent.

SSN noise. Clean SSNs are joined from the Social Security observer; some people never held one in the simulation, and those blanks are counted first. The file’s target share (20% for the finder files, 5% for the registry) is reached by blanking only the shortfall, so a file whose structural share already exceeds its target is left as it is, which is one mechanism with two outcomes. In the finder files 1% of the SSNs still present then have one randomly chosen adjacent pair of digits swapped, dashes preserved, which can produce a number outside the ranges the Social Security Administration issues. Both steps use one numpy generator per file, seeded with the file’s pseudopeople seed.

Row duplication and what switching it off does. pseudopeople’s duplicate-with-guardian mechanism copies a child’s or student’s record to a guardian’s address, giving one person two rows. It is set to zero here. Switching any pseudopeople mechanism off re-draws the cell noise across the whole file, because the cells to noise are chosen by a binomial draw over the number of eligible rows, so this release is a fresh realisation of the same design rather than the previous one minus a few rows.

Diagnosis date. A keyed hash of the identifier with seed 2026 places each registry record’s diagnosis on a day drawn uniformly within its census year, written as MM/DD/YYYY like the date of birth.

File formats and packaging. The files are UTF-8 CSV with a header row; blanks are empty fields, never a sentinel; dates are MM/DD/YYYY and SSNs ddd-dd-dddd; a field is quoted only when it contains a comma, which is rare enough that DuckDB’s CSV sniffer infers no quote character and fails unless it is named; addresses and cities are lower case, and unincorporated stands for unincorporated areas. The zip is written with fixed member timestamps and permissions, so its bytes depend only on its contents and its internal path, which carries the version; the data dictionary inside it has one row per field with type, format, example, blank convention, source and the noise mechanisms that touch it. The manifest lists rows, people and MD5 and SHA-256 digests for every file and the zip.

Definitions of the measures. A date of birth is unparseable when a strict MM/DD/YYYY parse fails; a Doe-pattern name is a first name of John or Jane with the last name Doe; an SSN is outside the issued ranges when its area is 000, 666 or 900 and above, its group 00 or its serial 0000. The exact-agreement rules compare values after lower-casing and trimming, each rule as a hash join between the registry and a finder file with disjunctions as unions, so the ladder runs in seconds without enumerating the pairs; precision and recall are scored against the identifier, with missed-match one minus recall and false-match one minus precision. The stratified baselines group the finder record’s race/ethnicity as White, Latino, Black, Asian, and other or unknown, the last pooling American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial or other, and blank. Blocking counts are the candidate pairs produced by joining the files on the key and the share of true pairs that share the key.
